title: How to choose between multiple hypotheses when coaching
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton addresses a recurring question from coaches he trains: when a lesson observation reveals many things to improve, which one should the coaching session target? Using his hypothesis model, in which an observer forms a testable prediction and gathers evidence, he lists six real hypotheses from one lesson. He argues firmly for picking a single focus, because several simultaneous changes overwhelm the teacher and make it impossible to see which change worked. He then weighs choosing the easiest win, which builds buy-in with sceptical or new teachers, against the highest-impact action, which often depends on prerequisites. Using Josh Goodrich's responsive-coaching sequence, he concludes that coaches should work through the order of dependencies, such as securing attention before refining checks for understanding.
points: Coaching should target one change at a time, since multiple changes overwhelm teachers and confound the cause of any improvement.
The easiest action is a good choice when the teacher is new to coaching, sceptical or low in confidence, because early success builds buy-in.
The highest-impact action cannot simply be leapfrogged to, because it usually rests on earlier foundations.
Goodrich's ordered framework lets a coach sequence priorities, here securing attention and clear explanation before improving checks for understanding in the We Do.
A slower, dependency-ordered approach yields more lasting change than jumping to the biggest lever.
quotes: Long-time readers will know I use the hypothesis model when observing a lesson. In short, I form a hypothesis about something in the lesson that is not going as well as it could be and then gather evidence to support or refute that hypothesis. This hypothesis forms the basis of the feedback and coaching session that follows.
The first thing to say is that we should resist the temptation to focus on more than one area. That is a mistake I made early on in my coaching journey.

One option is to choose the easiest action to implement. This approach may be appropriate if the teacher is new to coaching, sceptical, or lacks confidence. Picking a relatively easy action leads to the greatest chance of success, increasing buy-in and boosting confidence, setting you up for more impactful future coaching sessions.

Similarly, the teacher may have indicated an aspect of their teaching they would like to focus on - checking for understanding, or modelling, for example. In this case, choosing something from this area should increase buy-in and motivation.

This appears to be the obvious choice. However, there is a problem. Because that action may depend on other actions, trying to leap-frog these to get to the high-impact action risks everything falling down.

I think the action that will have the biggest impact on student learning is using mini-whiteboards to check for understanding during the We Do instead of Cold-Calling three students. This way, the teacher can assess the effort and understanding of all students instead of basing their assessment on a small sample.
